title: Distributed transactions
description: Learn about distributed transactions and the challenges of ACID across multiple services. Understand 2PC, sagas, and alternative approaches.

data.text: Distributed transactions coordinate updates across multiple databases or services while maintaining ACID properties. This is fundamentally difficult due to the CAP theorem and network uncertainty.
In a single database, transactions are easy—the database handles coordination. Across databases, you're on your own.

items: Network failures make coordination unreliable
CAP theorem limits consistency vs availability
Different databases have different transaction semantics
Coordination across services is complex
Performance overhead of distributed coordination

data.title: Avoid When Possible
data.text: Distributed transactions are expensive and complex. Avoid them by designing your system to minimize cross-service transactions.
2PC is a protocol for achieving atomic commitment across multiple participants.

items: Phase 1: Prepare—coordinator asks participants if they can commit
Phase 2: Commit or abort—based on participant responses
All participants must agree or all abort
Blocking protocol—participants hold locks during prepare
Single point of failure—the coordinator

data.title: Problems with 2PC
data.text: 2PC is blocking, slow, and has a single point of failure. It's rarely used in modern microservices due to these limitations.
Sagas break distributed transactions into a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions for rollback.

items: Execute local transactions in sequence
If a step fails, execute compensating transactions
Compensating actions undo previous steps
Eventually consistent—temporary inconsistency possible
Non-blocking—participants don't hold locks indefinitely

data.title: Recommended Approach
data.text: Sagas are the preferred approach for distributed transactions in microservices. They avoid the blocking and availability problems of 2PC.

items.title: Eventual Consistency
items.description: Accept temporary inconsistency. Use compensating actions to fix problems. Simplest but requires handling inconsistency.

items.title: TCC (Try-Confirm-Cancel)
items.description: Three-phase protocol with explicit try, confirm, and cancel operations. More complex but clearer semantics.

items.title: Outbox Pattern
items.description: Use outbox for reliable event publishing. Combine with idempotent consumers for eventual consistency.

items.title: Domain-Driven Design
items.description: Design bounded contexts to minimize cross-context transactions. Keep transactions within a single service when possible.

items: Avoid distributed transactions when possible
Design services to minimize cross-service operations
Use sagas for complex distributed workflows
Make operations idempotent to handle retries
Implement monitoring for saga execution
Document compensating actions clearly

data.text: Choose based on your consistency requirements and operational complexity tolerance.

items: 2PC: When you absolutely need strong consistency and can tolerate the complexity and performance cost
Sagas: When eventual consistency is acceptable and you want availability and scalability
Eventual consistency: When temporary inconsistency is acceptable and you want simplicity
No distributed transaction: When you can redesign to avoid the need entirely
